annotated_by: hand annotation, 2026-10-27, from the fixture text only (no parser output consulted while labelling)
matching_rule: A value counts as extracted when its normalised form (NFKC, casefold, whitespace collapsed, surrounding punctuation from ' \t.,;:|-/' stripped) equals the normalised expected form. Set semantics: a value is extracted or it is not; repeating it does not score twice.
empty_expectation_rule: If a field has no expected value in a fixture and the parser emits one, that emission is a false positive. This is how an abstention rule is made falsifiable: 'we do not guess' must be measurable.

fixtures.surface: single column, exact headings, marked bullets
fixtures.note: The reference case: everything the parser claims to do should work here.

fixtures.surface: synonym headings, 'Present' as an end marker, phone in the contact block
fixtures.note: An open-ended role must not invent an end year.

fixtures.surface: tab-separated role lines (flattened two-column)
fixtures.note: The layout damage is reported; the fields must still be recoverable from the same line.

fixtures.surface: heading vocabulary variants (ABOUT ME / EMPLOYMENT HISTORY / TECHNOLOGIES / ACADEMIC BACKGROUND)
fixtures.note: Heading synonyms are the cheap axis; a rename must not lose a field.

fixtures.surface: no headings at all; prose plus unmarked achievements
fixtures.note: Section-driven extraction must abstain, not infer. The year inside prose is the trap.

fixtures.surface: German headings, '03/2019 - heute' date style, umlauts
fixtures.note: Multilingual is a stated requirement (docs/02 2.6); this is the measurement of it.

fixtures.surface: French headings with accents, 'Présent', apostrophes
fixtures.note: Accented headings are the P1 class: an ASCII-only rule loses the whole section.

fixtures.surface: Greek headings and body, 'Simeras' end marker transliterated as希腊
fixtures.note: Non-Latin script: token equality, not translation, is what is being tested.

fixtures.surface: Spanish headings, 'Actualidad'
EXPERIENCE and SKILLS each appear twice (audit P5)
fixtures.note: First-heading-wins used to drop the second block silently. Both blocks must survive.

fixtures.surface: key-value role rows flattened with wide gaps (a table read as text)
achievements with no bullet marker (audit P4)
skills as bullets; one bullet names two tools
fixtures.note: '* git and docker' is one list item that carries two skills. Splitting on ' and ' in prose is a false-positive risk, so this fixture measures the gap rather than papering over it.

fixtures.surface: one contact value per line, plus a postal address
fixtures.note: A postal address is a location, not a contact channel; it must not be emitted as a contact.

fixtures.surface: a year inside summary prose, no skills section
fixtures.note: A year in a sentence is not an employment date. The expected list proves the rule; the forbidden list makes it falsifiable.

fixtures.surface: single role, no education section, lowercase 'present'
everything upper-cased, including the email
Irish headings, accented personal names, 'inniu'
fixtures.note: A name with prefixes (O, Do) is the P1 tokenisation case in real use.

fixtures.surface: employers named in prose and in a reference block
fixtures.note: An employer mentioned inside a bullet, and a reference's employer and email, are not the candidate's employer or contact channel.

fixtures.surface: no blank lines, soft hyphens inside words, '2013/2019' date style, Dutch 'heden'
employer-first role line ('Norra Bank - Senior Engineer')
fixtures.note: ADVERSARIAL. The parser assumes title-first, so both fields come out swapped. This fixture exists to keep the headline number honest, not to be fixed by a tie-breaker we cannot justify.

fixtures.surface: role line with the date on the following line
fixtures.note: ADVERSARIAL. The role-line rule needs the date on the same line; with it elsewhere the line is unrecognised and the employer/title are lost while the years survive.

fixtures.surface: skills as a two-column table (category tab list)
fixtures.note: ADVERSARIAL. A table read as text puts the category word and the whole list on one line; the split then produces one compound value per row.

fixtures.surface: a headline line above the name
fixtures.note: ADVERSARIAL. The name rule stops at the first non-channel line; that line here is a job title. A small headline-word list makes the rule emit no name, an abstention. Before that guard the parser reported 'SENIOR SECURITY ENGINEER' as the candidate's name: a wrong value, which is the failure class that matters most here.

fixtures.surface: skill table with a level column
fixtures.note: ADVERSARIAL, added 2026-10-27 for the table orientation the splitter cannot resolve. A reader lists Python and Kubernetes as the skills; 'Advanced' and 'Expert' are levels, not skills. `skill_items` drops a first cell only when the second cell is a list and the first names a class of skill, so a level column produces two extra skill facts. Left failing on purpose: adding a level vocabulary to make this pass would be tuning the corpus, not reading tables. The 2013 education year is labelled as everywhere else in the corpus; the first version of this label omitted it and the parser scored two false positives that were its own annotation's fault.

fixtures.surface: employer-first line with no naming evidence
fixtures.note: ADVERSARIAL, added 2026-10-27. The first version of this fixture said 'Scrum Master' and passed the moment 'scrum' entered the role-evidence vocabulary - it measured the vocabulary, not the convention. 'Release Steward' is a real title made of words the list has never seen, so neither segment carries evidence, the documented title-first default stands, and this entry comes out transposed: one false employer, one false title, while the second entry ('Release Steward, Verode') is right by the same rule. That is M-6 in one labelled document: what is missing is not a word list but the frequency of the employer-first convention in real CVs. The 2016 education year is labelled as everywhere else in the corpus.

job_descriptions.note: The responsibilities line is not an ask and is excluded; 'WHAT YOU WILL NEED' and 'NICE TO HAVE' are headings, not requirements, and count 0.
'Python is not required' contains the cue word 'required' and must not be classified must.

job_descriptions.surface: one line that is both desirable and required elsewhere
job_descriptions.note: Where the cues contradict, the honest answer is unknown, not whichever cue the loop saw first.

job_descriptions.surface: a requirements section with no obligation words at all
job_descriptions.note: Membership of the section is the only signal; the weight must stay unknown.

job_descriptions.surface: the same requirement repeated under two headings
job_descriptions.note: Repetition is not two asks. Duplicates must collapse.

ADVERSARIAL, and the most important one here: both vocabularies - headings and cues - are English, so a German advertisement yields no requirements at all (not even unknown-weighted ones). The expected row is what a reader of the text would label, not what our rule finds.

Second non-English advertisement, added so the 'n=1 per language' ceiling in docs/08 M-9 does not apply to advertisements. Labels are what a reader of the text would write: 'indispensable' is an obligation cue, 'souhaitée' a preference cue, and 'Vous avez une expérience …' asserts a requirement without a cue word. The parser finds all three requirements and weights two of them `unknown`, because no cue list covers that assertive phrasing - recorded as a limit, not fixed by re-labelling.

anchor_jd.note: Fixed advertisement used by the stability measurement, so cosine drift is measured against one constant.

name_rule: The name is the first contact-block line that is not an email, URL, phone or location. A CV that puts its name somewhere else is not covered by the rule, and no fixture in this set tests that; docs/08 records it as unmeasured.
